questions.title: How does the 'substantial prejudice' standard for harmless error work in practice?
questions.question_body: The court mentions that they won't reverse a conviction for an erroneous ruling if the error was 'harmless' and only reverse if the jury may have been 'substantially swayed.' I'm confused about what 'substantially swayed' actually looks like. If there is some evidence of a mistake, but the government also has DNA evidence and multiple witnesses, does that automatically mean the error is harmless? How do courts quantify that 'swing' in the jury's mind?

questions.title: Why is testimony about prior possession of a gun considered 'intrinsic evidence' rather than 'propensity evidence' under Rule 404(b)?
questions.question_body: The defendant argued that the witnesses testifying about seeing him with the gun in the past was propensity evidence (i.e., 'he had a gun before, so he is the type of person who would have a gun now'). However, the court ruled it was 'intrinsic evidence' relevant to proving current possession. Can you explain the distinction? Why does 'ownership or control' of a specific item bypass the usual 404(b) restrictions on character evidence?

questions.title: If a witness testifies in person, does that automatically cure all hearsay issues regarding their prior statements to police?
questions.question_body: The court refused to give a limiting instruction regarding D.F.'s statements to the police because she eventually testified in person, satisfying the Confrontation Clause. However, I'm still confused about the hearsay aspect. If she said X to the police but didn't mention X during her live testimony, can the jury still consider X as 'substantive evidence' just because she is physically present in the room?

questions.title: Why was the police report excluded as extrinsic evidence for impeachment even though it contained the witness's own statements?
questions.question_body: The defense wanted to use a police report to impeach C.F. because she gave a different story than what was in the report. The court blocked this because the report wasn't 'authored' by her. If the report is just a record of what she said to the officer, why does it fail the authentication requirement for extrinsic evidence? Why can't the defense just read the part she said?

questions.title: How can a sentence be 'within the guidelines' but still be argued as violating the 'sufficient, but not greater than necessary' principle of 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a)?
questions.question_body: The defendant argues that the 4-level enhancement makes his sentence 'greater than necessary' under § 3553(a), even though the final sentence fell within the resulting guideline range. If the Guidelines are designed to be the starting point for a 'sufficient' sentence, how can a sentence stay inside those bounds but still be 'too much'? Is this a procedural argument about the calculation of the range, or a substantive argument about the judge's discretion?

questions.title: When the Armed Career Criminal Act (ACCA) and a specific USSG enhancement both apply, how is the final offense level determined?
questions.question_body: In this case, the ACCA would have resulted in an offense level of 34, but the USSG § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) enhancement resulted in a level of 35. The court applied the higher level. Is there a general rule that the 'greater' enhancement always wins, or does the court have to weigh the specific purposes of the ACCA against the US Sentencing Guidelines?
